nodes.name: Algal biomass
nodes.description: Algal biomass — from freshwater microalgae (Chlorella, Spirulina), marine macroalgae (seaweeds), or photobioreactor cultivation — is among the highest-productivity biomass sources per unit area. Microalgae can accumulate 20–50% lipid content under nutrient stress, making them attractive for oil extraction and hydrothermal liquefaction. The energy cost of cultivation, harvesting, and dewatering remains the primary barrier to commercial-scale production.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: High potential productivity; can use brackish water and non-arable land; water and energy requirements for dewatering are significant.

nodes.name: Sugarcane bagasse
nodes.description: Sugarcane bagasse is the fibrous residue remaining after juice extraction from sugarcane stalks, comprising roughly 25–30% of the cane mass as pressed wet material. It is generated at centralized sugar mills, making it one of the most logistics-ready lignocellulosic feedstocks. Brazil and other tropical countries use it extensively for combined heat and power at the mill, and it is also processed via enzymatic hydrolysis for second-generation ethanol or via thermochemical routes.
current_disposal: burned for process energy at mill
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Generated as a mill co-product with no additional land-use impact; high moisture requires drying for thermochemical routes.

nodes.name: Corn stover
nodes.description: Corn stover is the non-grain portion of the corn plant — stalks, leaves, husks, and cobs — left on the field after harvest. It is one of the most abundant agricultural residues in North America, with the US generating roughly 250–350 million dry tonnes per year. As a dry lignocellulosic feedstock it suits both thermochemical conversion (pyrolysis, gasification) and biochemical routes (enzymatic hydrolysis after pretreatment). Collection rates are typically capped at 30–60% of available material to preserve soil organic matter.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Removing stover depletes soil organic carbon and increases erosion risk; sustainable harvest rates depend on soil type and management practice.

nodes.name: Post-consumer food waste
nodes.description: Post-consumer food waste is the mixed organic residue discarded by households, restaurants, cafeterias, and retailers. It is highly heterogeneous — a mixture of proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and water — making targeted pretreatment difficult. Anaerobic digestion is the most established pathway, converting the mixed organics to biogas regardless of composition. The wet fraction also carries lipid content suitable for mechanical separation when source-separated.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Diverting food waste from landfill avoids methane emissions; collection and sorting infrastructure is a key barrier.

nodes.name: Livestock manure
nodes.description: Livestock manure — from dairy cattle, swine, poultry, and other farm animals — is one of the most widely distributed organic waste streams globally. Its high moisture content (>80% for liquid slurries) and rich nutrient composition make anaerobic digestion the natural conversion pathway, producing biogas and nutrient-rich digestate. Unmanaged manure storage is a significant agricultural source of methane and nitrous oxide, so biogas capture provides both energy and emissions abatement.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Biogas capture from manure provides strong GHG benefits; ammonia emissions during storage and spreading are a key air quality concern.

nodes.name: MSW organic fraction
nodes.description: The municipal solid waste (MSW) organic fraction is the biogenic portion of household and commercial waste after separation from plastics, glass, and metals. Quality varies significantly: source-separated 'green bin' waste is far more consistent than mechanically separated MSW. Contaminants (plastics, soil, pathogens) must be managed in any conversion process, particularly when the output is a soil amendment applied to agricultural land.

nodes.sustainability_considerations: Contamination from non-organic fractions can limit product quality; regulatory standards for compost and digestate vary by jurisdiction.

nodes.name: Oilseed crop waste
nodes.description: Oilseed crops — rapeseed, soybean, sunflower, and palm — yield a triglyceride-rich oil fraction when cold-pressed or solvent-extracted, with the residual protein-rich press cake (30–50% protein) primarily used as animal feed. The lipid fraction routes directly to biodiesel via transesterification or to renewable diesel and SAF via hydrotreating. Dedicated oilseed crops compete with food production for productive agricultural land, raising sustainability questions that waste-stream lipid feedstocks avoid.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Land-use competition with food and feed; lifecycle emissions depend heavily on whether indirect land-use change is included.

nodes.name: Protein-rich waste
nodes.description: Protein-rich organic wastes include slaughterhouse offal, fish processing residues, dairy whey, insect frass, and fermentation residues with high protein content. These materials contain amino acids recoverable via enzymatic hydrolysis for specialty chemicals, animal feed supplements, or nitrogen sources for fermentation. Anaerobic digestion is also viable, though the high nitrogen content can cause ammonia inhibition at elevated loading rates.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Animal-derived waste streams carry pathogen risks requiring heat treatment; regulations on use as animal feed are strict in many jurisdictions.

nodes.name: WWTP sludge
nodes.description: Wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) sludge is the solid residue from municipal sewage treatment, rich in microbial biomass, undigested organic matter, and nutrients (especially nitrogen and phosphorus). Primary sludge is the settleable solids removed early in treatment; secondary (activated) sludge is the biological mass cultivated to break down dissolved organics. Anaerobic digestion of sludge is the most established bioconversion pathway, recovering biogas while producing stabilized digestate.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Sludge may contain micropollutants, heavy metals, and pathogens requiring treatment; regulatory limits on land application vary by country.

nodes.name: Brewery spent grain
nodes.description: Brewery spent grain (BSG) is the residual malt and barley husk remaining after wort extraction in beer production — roughly 20 kg per 100 L of beer produced. Its wet composition is approximately 75% moisture, 15–25% protein, and 15–25% lignocellulosic fiber on a dry basis. Historically used as cattle feed, BSG is increasingly seen as a higher-value feedstock for biochemical conversion given its protein and fermentable carbohydrate content.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Very short shelf life due to high moisture; collection logistics from dispersed small breweries can be challenging.

nodes.name: Starchy food waste
nodes.description: Starchy food waste encompasses starch-rich organic residues from food processing and consumption — including expired baked goods, potato processing waste, and cafeteria carbohydrate waste. Unlike lignocellulosic feedstocks, starch is readily hydrolyzed to glucose without extensive pretreatment, making these materials particularly accessible to fermentation pathways. Sugar-rich fractions such as fruit processing waste and molasses fall in the same conversion category.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Using food waste avoids landfill methane emissions; does not compete with food production.

nodes.name: Switchgrass
nodes.description: Switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) is a warm-season perennial grass native to North America, cultivated as a dedicated energy crop for its high lignocellulosic yield and low input requirements. It grows on marginal land unsuitable for food crops and sequesters carbon deeply in its extensive root system. Annual dry matter yields of 5–15 tonnes per hectare make it one of the best-studied energy crops, though commercial-scale biorefinery deployment remains limited.
current_disposal: not yet at commercial scale — still predominantly a research crop
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Lower lifecycle emissions than annual crops; can improve soil health on degraded land; no displacement of food production on marginal sites.

nodes.name: Used cooking oil
nodes.description: Used cooking oil (UCO) is the triglyceride-rich oil recovered from restaurants, food processors, and households after cooking. It is one of the most economically attractive biofuel feedstocks — already collected in many municipalities, low in production cost, and well-suited to transesterification (FAME biodiesel) or hydrotreating (renewable diesel and SAF). The EU's Renewable Energy Directive grants UCO-derived fuels double-counting credits, creating strong policy incentives for collection.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Strong sustainability profile as a true waste stream with no land-use impact; supply is geographically dispersed and collection infrastructure varies widely.

nodes.name: Wheat straw
nodes.description: Wheat straw is the dry stem and leaf residue from wheat harvesting, generated at roughly 1:1 mass ratio with grain yield. It is among the most abundant crop residues in Europe, Asia, and North America. Like other lignocellulosic feedstocks, it requires pretreatment before enzymatic hydrolysis because the lignin and hemicellulose matrix restricts enzyme access. Some straw is left on fields for soil conditioning, limiting collection rates to roughly 40–60%.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Straw removal affects soil carbon balance and erosion; competes with bedding and animal-feed uses.

nodes.name: Forestry residue
nodes.description: Forestry residues are the woody biomass left after logging operations and at sawmills — branches, treetops, bark, and offcuts. With cellulose 40–50%, hemicellulose 20–30%, and lignin 20–30%, they are a high-quality lignocellulosic feedstock. Relatively high lignin content and varied species composition require robust pretreatment for biochemical routes. Harvesting must be balanced against maintaining forest soil organic matter and deadwood habitat for biodiversity.
nodes.sustainability_considerations: Removing residues reduces habitat for saproxylic species and can deplete soil nutrients; sustainable extraction limits apply.

nodes.name: AFEX
nodes.description: Ammonia fiber expansion (AFEX) exposes moist biomass to anhydrous ammonia under pressure at moderate temperature (70–120°C), then rapidly releases pressure to cause explosive decompression. Unlike acid and steam explosion, AFEX produces very few inhibitory compounds and requires no washing step, making the treated solid directly accessible to enzymes and fermentation organisms. Ammonia recovery and recycling is essential for both process economics and environmental safety.
nodes.mechanism_brief: Anhydrous liquid ammonia applied to moist biomass (70–120°C) swells and disrupts the lignocellulosic structure through combined chemical and physical action; rapid pressure release then explosively defibrillates cell walls.
environmental_impacts: high capital cost for pressure vessels

nodes.name: Alkaline (NaOH / lime)
nodes.description: Alkaline pretreatment with sodium hydroxide or lime disrupts lignin–carbohydrate ester bonds and removes acetyl groups from hemicellulose, swelling the cellulose structure and improving cellulase accessibility. nodes.name: Fungal pretreatment

The major drawback is time: fungal colonization typically requires 1–4 weeks, making continuous industrial-scale processing impractical at current development stage.

Composting returns carbon to the soil rather than capturing it as energy.

nodes.name: Fast pyrolysis
nodes.description: Fast pyrolysis uses very rapid heating rates (100–10,000°C/s) and short vapor residence times (<2 s) to maximize bio-oil yield — typically 60–75% on a dry mass basis. Fast pyrolysis is particularly well-suited to dry lignocellulosic feedstocks and is among the more commercially advanced non-combustion thermochemical routes.
nodes.mechanism_brief: Very rapid heating (100–10,000°C/s) to 400–600°C with short vapor residence times (<2 s) and immediate quenching maximizes condensable bio-oil vapors at the expense of char and non-condensable gas.

nodes.name: Hydrothermal liquefaction
nodes.description: Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) converts wet biomass into a crude bio-oil (biocrude) by processing it in pressurized liquid water at elevated temperatures (250–374°C). Because water acts as both solvent and reactant, HTL can process high-moisture feedstocks — algae, sludge, food waste — without the energy-intensive pre-drying required by most thermochemical routes. The bio-oil product requires upgrading via hydrotreating to meet fuel specifications.
nodes.mechanism_brief: Wet biomass is processed at 250–374°C and 10–25 MPa in subcritical liquid water; at these conditions water's ionic product and dielectric constant shift dramatically, enabling depolymerization and repolymerization reactions that convert biomass macromolecules to bio-oil.

nodes.name: Direct saccharification
nodes.description: Direct saccharification converts starch-rich materials to fermentable glucose sugars using amylase enzymes (α-amylase for liquefaction, glucoamylase for saccharification). Unlike cellulosic conversion, starch hydrolysis does not require intensive physical or chemical pretreatment — the α-glycosidic bonds in starch are far more accessible to enzymes than the β-glycosidic bonds in cellulose. This is the basis of conventional corn-to-ethanol fermentation and is a well-established industrial process globally.
nodes.mechanism_brief: α-Amylase (liquefaction at 90–105°C) and glucoamylase (saccharification at 60°C) sequentially hydrolyze starch α-1,4 and α-1,6 glycosidic bonds to produce a glucose syrup ready for fermentation.

nodes.name: Slow pyrolysis
nodes.description: Slow pyrolysis thermally decomposes biomass at 300–500°C under inert atmosphere with slow heating rates (1–20°C/min) and long residence times, favoring biochar production. All three pyrolysis products — biochar, bio-oil, and syngas — are generated simultaneously in proportions that shift with temperature and residence time. The syngas byproduct is typically combusted to provide process heat, and bio-oil is a secondary liquid of lower quality than fast pyrolysis bio-oil.
nodes.mechanism_brief: Slow thermal decomposition at 300–500°C with slow heating rates (1–20°C/min) and long residence times (hours) maximizes biochar yield by allowing secondary char-forming reactions to proceed.

nodes.name: Torrefaction
nodes.description: Torrefaction is mild pyrolysis (200–300°C) in the absence of oxygen that partially decomposes biomass, removing moisture and degrading hemicellulose while preserving most energy content in a more energy-dense solid. The torrefied product is hydrophobic, brittle, and easier to grind — properties that make it a better co-firing fuel for coal plants or a more homogeneous feedstock for gasification. Mass loss is 20–30% but energy loss is typically only 10%.
nodes.mechanism_brief: Thermal treatment at 200–300°C under inert atmosphere decomposes hemicellulose and surface hydroxyl groups, producing a hydrophobic, grindable, energy-dense solid with 20–30% higher energy density than raw biomass.

nodes.name: Amino acids
nodes.description: Amino acids are the monomeric building blocks of proteins, recovered by enzymatic hydrolysis of protein-rich waste streams. As a platform, they represent a high-value chemical intermediate with applications in food, feed, pharmaceuticals, and as precursors for specialty chemicals. The composition of the amino acid mixture depends on the protein source — different proteins have characteristic amino acid profiles that determine downstream applications and market value.

nodes.name: Bio-oil
nodes.description: Bio-oil (pyrolysis liquid) is a complex, dark brown liquid produced by condensing the vapors from fast or slow pyrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass. It contains hundreds of oxygenated organic compounds — organic acids, phenolics, ketones, aldehydes, and sugars — with a water content of 20–30%. Raw bio-oil has lower energy density and higher oxygen content than petroleum, and its acidity and instability limit direct use as a drop-in fuel. Upgrading via hydrotreating reduces oxygen content and improves fuel properties.

nodes.name: Biochar
nodes.description: Biochar is a carbon-rich solid produced by pyrolysis or hydrothermal carbonization of biomass in the absence or limited presence of oxygen. Its highly porous structure and stable aromatic carbon matrix give it distinctive soil amendment properties — improving water retention, cation exchange capacity, and microbial habitat. When incorporated into soil, biochar sequesters carbon on timescales of centuries, making it one of the few bioenergy products with a negative carbon footprint.

nodes.name: Biogas
nodes.description: Biogas is the gas mixture produced by anaerobic digestion — typically 55–70% methane and 30–45% carbon dioxide, with trace amounts of hydrogen sulfide and ammonia. Raw biogas can be combusted directly for heat and power. When upgraded to remove CO₂ and contaminants, it becomes biomethane — compositionally equivalent to natural gas and injectable into the gas grid. Biogas is one of the most versatile and widely deployed bioenergy platforms, compatible with a broad range of wet organic feedstocks.

nodes.name: Digestate
nodes.description: Digestate is the residual material remaining after anaerobic digestion — the non-gasified portion that retains most of the feedstock's nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in plant-available forms. It can be applied directly to agricultural land as a biofertilizer, replacing synthetic nitrogen fertilizer. Solid-liquid separation allows the nutrient-rich liquid fraction to be applied separately, adapting the product for different farm management systems.

nodes.name: Process heat & power
nodes.description: Process heat and power is the thermal energy platform generated within a biorefinery — the steam, hot gases, and electricity used to drive other unit operations. In a combustion- or gasification-based biorefinery, excess heat beyond internal demand can be exported to adjacent facilities or used to generate electricity via a steam turbine. This platform is distinct from the exported energy products: here, the energy is being used inside the conversion process.

nodes.name: Hydrogen
nodes.description: Hydrogen is a pure gas intermediate produced from biomass via gasification followed by water-gas shift, or from biogas via steam methane reforming, or directly from anaerobic fermentation under modified conditions. As a platform, it routes to fuel cells for electricity generation or to chemical synthesis — notably ammonia. Biomass-derived hydrogen from waste or residual feedstocks qualifies as renewable, though production costs remain higher than fossil-derived hydrogen.

nodes.name: Lignin
nodes.description: Lignin is the complex aromatic polymer that binds cellulose and hemicellulose in the plant cell wall, comprising 15–35% of lignocellulosic biomass. In enzymatic hydrolysis processes, it remains as a solid residue after sugars are extracted. While most current commercial processes burn lignin for internal heat and power, it is an underexplored platform for aromatic chemicals, carbon fiber precursors, and bio-adhesives — applications that could dramatically improve biorefinery economics as valorization pathways mature.

nodes.name: Stabilized organic matter
nodes.description: Stabilized organic matter is the mature, biologically stable product of aerobic composting — a dark, earthy material rich in humic substances that forms the basis of compost. Unlike fresh organic waste, it resists further microbial decomposition, making it safe and beneficial to apply to soils. It improves soil structure, water retention, and biological activity while serving as a slow-release nutrient source.

nodes.name: C5 / C6 sugars
nodes.description: C5 and C6 sugars are the fermentable monosaccharides liberated from cellulose and hemicellulose by enzymatic hydrolysis or saccharification. Glucose (C6) is readily fermented by conventional yeast to ethanol; pentose sugars (xylose, arabinose — C5) require engineered microorganisms. The C5:C6 ratio depends on feedstock composition — softwoods yield mostly C6, agricultural residues yield significant C5 fractions that must be co-fermented for efficient yields.

nodes.name: Syngas
nodes.description: Syngas (synthesis gas) is a mixture of carbon monoxide (CO) and hydrogen (H₂), with varying amounts of CO₂ and methane, produced by gasification or reforming. The H₂:CO ratio is a critical quality parameter determining downstream upgrading options — Fischer-Tropsch synthesis prefers 2:1 H₂:CO, while methanol synthesis requires ~3:1. Syngas requires cleanup to remove tar, particulates, and sulfur compounds before use in sensitive catalytic processes.

nodes.name: Vegetable / algal oil
nodes.description: Vegetable and algal oils are triglyceride-rich lipid fractions extracted from oilseed crops, used cooking oil, microalgae, or lipid-rich food waste. As a platform intermediate, these oils serve as feedstock for both transesterification (producing FAME biodiesel) and hydrotreating (producing renewable diesel or SAF). Fatty acid composition — types and chain lengths — varies by source and determines the quality and cold-flow properties of the resulting fuel.

nodes.name: Volatile fatty acids
nodes.description: Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) are short-chain organic acids (C2–C6) produced as intermediates in the acidogenesis stage of anaerobic digestion, or as primary products when methanogenesis is deliberately suppressed. They can be further converted to biogas, concentrated as platform chemicals, or chain-elongated to medium-chain fatty acids through specific fermentation routes. VFA production is gaining attention as a way to extract higher-value chemicals from complex organic waste streams.

nodes.name: Biogas upgrading
nodes.description: Biogas upgrading removes CO₂ and trace contaminants from raw biogas to produce biomethane — a gas compositionally equivalent to natural gas (>96% CH₄). Multiple proven technologies are available: pressure swing adsorption (PSA), water scrubbing, membrane separation, and chemical absorption with amines. Biomethane can be injected directly into existing natural gas grid infrastructure, enabling large-scale renewable gas distribution without requiring new end-use infrastructure.
nodes.mechanism_brief: CO₂ is selectively removed from raw biogas (55–70% CH₄) using pressure swing adsorption (PSA), water scrubbing, membrane separation, or amine absorption, yielding >96% CH₄ biomethane meeting grid injection standards.

nodes.name: Hydrotreating
nodes.description: Hydrotreating removes oxygen, sulfur, and nitrogen from bio-oil or vegetable oil feedstocks by reacting them with high-pressure hydrogen over a NiMo or CoMo catalyst. For vegetable oils, this hydrodeoxygenation produces hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids (HEFA) — one of the most commercially advanced SAF pathways. Hydrotreating is co-processable at existing petroleum refineries, which lowers entry costs compared to greenfield biofuel plants.
nodes.mechanism_brief: High-pressure hydrogen (50–200 bar) at 300–450°C reacts with oxygenated bio-oil or triglycerides over a NiMo or CoMo catalyst; deoxygenation reactions remove oxygen as water or CO₂ while dehydrogenation and isomerization improve fuel properties.

nodes.name: Transesterification
nodes.description: Transesterification reacts triglycerides (vegetable or algal oil) with methanol in the presence of a base catalyst (NaOH or KOH) at 55–65°C to produce fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) — biodiesel — and glycerol as a co-product. It is the most commercially mature biodiesel production process, with thousands of plants worldwide. FAME biodiesel can be blended with petroleum diesel up to B20 without engine modifications, or used at higher concentrations in adapted vehicles.
nodes.mechanism_brief: Triglycerides react with methanol at a ~6:1 molar ratio in the presence of NaOH or KOH catalyst at 55–65°C; each ester bond in the triglyceride is transesterified with a methanol molecule, releasing glycerol and producing three fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) molecules.

nodes.name: Bio-adhesives
nodes.description: Bio-adhesives are adhesive products derived from lignin, tannins, proteins, or bio-based resins that substitute for formaldehyde-based and petrochemical adhesives. Lignin-based adhesives for wood composites are the most commercially advanced, driven by formaldehyde's indoor air quality concerns and the availability of lignin as a biorefinery residue. Protein-based adhesives from soy meal are well-established for specific wood-product applications.

nodes.name: Biochar soil amendment
nodes.description: Biochar applied to agricultural or degraded soils improves physical, chemical, and biological soil properties. Its porous structure improves water and nutrient retention, its alkalinity can correct acidic soils, and its recalcitrant carbon is stable in soil for centuries — making it the primary pathway to bioenergy with long-term carbon removal. Effects on crop yields are highly variable depending on soil type, application rate, and the feedstock from which the biochar was produced.

nodes.name: Biodiesel (FAME)
nodes.description: Biodiesel (fatty acid methyl ester, FAME) is produced by transesterification of vegetable oils or animal fats with methanol. It is the most commercially mature biofuel globally, with established standards (EN 14214 in Europe, ASTM D6751 in the US) and widespread blending infrastructure. FAME biodiesel has slightly lower energy density than petroleum diesel and can cause issues at high blend ratios in cold climates, but blends up to B20 are supported by most engine manufacturers.

nodes.name: Grid biomethane
nodes.description: Grid biomethane is upgraded biogas meeting natural gas grid injection specifications — typically >96% CH₄ and <50 ppm H₂S. Once injected into the natural gas grid, it is indistinguishable from fossil gas and can be used by any gas appliance or in gas vehicles. It represents a fully fungible renewable gas that leverages existing gas infrastructure without requiring modifications at the point of use.

nodes.name: Bioplastics (PLA / PHA)
nodes.description: Bio-based and/or biodegradable plastics — primarily polylactic acid (PLA) from lactic acid fermentation and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHA) from microbial fermentation of sugars or VFAs — substitute for fossil plastics with lower lifecycle carbon footprints. PLA is produced commercially from corn or sugarcane sugars for food packaging and disposable items. PHA is produced by bacteria accumulating it as an intracellular carbon reserve and remains more expensive than conventional plastics.

nodes.name: Carbon fiber
nodes.description: Bio-based carbon fiber can be produced by thermally processing lignin or cellulose-based precursors into high-strength graphitic filaments. Lignin — available as a low-cost biorefinery co-product — is being explored as a precursor for lower-cost carbon fiber, which currently commands high prices ($20–100/kg) due to energy-intensive production from petroleum-derived acrylonitrile. Bio-based carbon fiber remains at pilot scale, with mechanical performance not yet fully equivalent to PAN-derived fiber.

nodes.name: Compost
nodes.description: Compost is the mature product of aerobic composting — a stable, humus-rich organic amendment that improves soil structure, water retention, and biological activity. It replaces or supplements synthetic fertilizers and peat in horticulture and agriculture. Unlike digestate, compost is dry, pathogen-free, and odor-reduced — properties that make it compatible with retail distribution and use by non-specialist growers.
nodes.fossil_analog: Peat (as soil conditioner) / synthetic fertilizers (as nutrient source)

nodes.name: Digestate fertilizer
nodes.description: Digestate fertilizer is processed digestate from anaerobic digestion applied to agricultural land as a nutrient-rich biofertilizer. It contains most of the feedstock's nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium in plant-available forms — particularly ammonium nitrogen immediately accessible to crops. Unlike composting, anaerobic digestion preserves nitrogen rather than mineralizing it, giving digestate higher immediate fertilizer value. Solid-liquid separation adapts the product for different application methods.
nodes.fossil_analog: Mineral nitrogen fertilizers (urea, ammonium nitrate, triple superphosphate)

nodes.name: Electricity
nodes.description: Electricity generated from bioenergy conversion — via steam turbine (combustion or gasification), gas engine (biogas), or fuel cell (hydrogen) — can be fed to the electricity grid or used on-site. Bioenergy power is dispatchable unlike solar and wind, making it a valuable grid asset for balancing variable renewable generation. Efficiency ranges from 20–25% (small plants) to 40–45% for large combined-cycle configurations.
nodes.fossil_analog: Coal and natural gas power plants

nodes.name: Ethanol
nodes.description: Bioethanol is produced by fermentation of sugars or starch and is the most widely produced biofuel globally — primarily from corn (US), sugarcane (Brazil), and increasingly from lignocellulosic biomass. It can be blended with gasoline (E10, E85) or used in flex-fuel vehicles at any concentration. Beyond fuel, ethanol is a platform chemical for producing ethylene (for plastics) and other derivatives, giving it dual energy-chemical value.

nodes.name: Fuel cell electricity
nodes.description: Fuel cell electricity is produced by electrochemically oxidizing hydrogen in a fuel cell, converting chemical energy directly to electricity without combustion, at efficiencies of 45–60%. Polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) fuel cells are most common for hydrogen; molten carbonate and solid oxide fuel cells can use biogas directly. Fuel cells are attractive for distributed power and transport applications where high efficiency and zero local emissions are valued.

nodes.name: Green ammonia
nodes.description: Green ammonia is produced by reacting hydrogen (from renewable sources including biomass gasification) with atmospheric nitrogen via the Haber-Bosch process, powered by renewable electricity. Ammonia is a critical nitrogen fertilizer feedstock and is increasingly explored as a carbon-free energy carrier for maritime shipping and long-duration energy storage. Biomass-derived hydrogen can serve as the feedstock, connecting the bioenergy and chemical sectors.
nodes.fossil_analog: Fossil-derived ammonia (Haber-Bosch process with natural gas steam reforming)

nodes.name: Heat
nodes.description: Heat is the simplest and most direct energy product from bioenergy — thermal energy delivered as steam, hot water, or flue gas for space heating, process heat, or district heating networks. Unlike electricity, heat cannot be economically transported over long distances, so bioenergy heat plants are typically sited near demand. Combined heat and power (CHP) configurations capture both heat and electricity from a single conversion process, substantially improving overall energy efficiency.
nodes.fossil_analog: Natural gas / district heating from fossil fuels

nodes.name: Med-chain fatty acids
nodes.description: Medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs, C6–C12) are produced by chain elongation of volatile fatty acids using specific anaerobic bacteria (e.g., Clostridium kluyveri). They have antimicrobial properties valuable as animal feed additives and food preservatives, and are precursors for bio-based surfactants and lubricants. MCFA production from VFAs represents a high-value upgrading pathway for mixed organic waste that improves the economics over biogas alone.

nodes.name: Renewable diesel
nodes.description: Renewable diesel is a drop-in fuel produced by hydrotreating vegetable oils or bio-oil, yielding a paraffinic hydrocarbon product with superior properties to FAME biodiesel — higher energy density, better cold-flow characteristics, and compatibility at any blend level with petroleum diesel. Unlike biodiesel, renewable diesel is chemically identical to petroleum diesel and requires no modifications to engines or fuel infrastructure.

nodes.name: Sustainable aviation fuel
nodes.description: Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is a drop-in jet fuel from renewable feedstocks meeting ASTM D7566 specification, blendable with conventional Jet A at up to 50% without aircraft modifications. Aviation is among the hardest sectors to decarbonize — long-haul routes cannot be electrified — making SAF a high-priority advanced biofuel. HEFA (from fats and oils) and FT (from syngas) are the two most developed pathways, achieving 50–80% lifecycle GHG reductions versus fossil jet fuel.

nodes.name: Specialty chemicals
nodes.description: Specialty chemicals from biomass encompass a range of high-value compounds — including itaconic acid, succinic acid, lactic acid derivatives, aromatic chemicals from lignin, and biochemicals from amino acid fermentation. These products command significantly higher prices per tonne than biofuels, making them economically attractive at smaller scales. The term covers bio-based chemicals that are not commodity chemicals or fuels — the 'high value' in the biorefinery value pyramid.
